newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Koreans call on Kim to sack aides over scandal.
newsitem.headline: S.Koreans call on Kim to sack aides over scandal.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam faced mounting pressure on Thursday to sack top officials after bankers were lined up for a prosecution probe into business kickbacks over a loan scandal, officials and analysts said.

"President Kim will have to carry out a major reshuffle of the cabinet and his ruling party but such a move will follow the end of the current probe into Hanbo loans," a senior government official said.
State prosecutors on Thursday summoned two more leading bankers in connection with massive loans to insolvent Hanbo Steel Co, flagship of the nation's 14th largest conglomerate.

A prosecution official told reporters that Chang Myung-son, president of the Korea Exchange Bank, and Kim Shi-hyung, head of the state-run Korea Development Bank, were being questioned by investigators on whether they were involved in irregularities.
On Wednesday, prosecutors arrested the heads of two other leading banks -- Sheen Kwang-shik of Korea First Bank and Woo Chan-mok of Cho Hung Bank -- on charges of bribery.
Lee Chong-yeon and Rhee Chul-soo, former heads of Cho Hung and Korea First, were also being questioned by prosecutors, the prosecution official said.

The four banks are the main creditors of Hanbo Steel, South Korea's second largest steelmaker, which was declared insolvent on January 23 after racking up about five trillion won ($5.8 billion) in loans.
Wednesday's arrests bring to 18 the number of bankers jailed or forced to resign since Kim swept to power in 1993 on an anti-graft platform.
Most were found to have accepted bribes from borrowers.

In a separate corruption case, a former head of SEOULBANK, one of South Korea's seven largest banks, was jailed for three years for taking 160 million won ($184,000) in commission in return for offering loans to a valve-making company.

"It is not possible to keep powerful officials at the (presidential) Blue House, party and government in their places while their moral credibility and management ability have collapsed," an editorial of leading daily Chosun Ilbo said.
President Kim, who ordered a probe into the loans last week, has said the Hanbo scandal is a typical example of corruption that is still widespread despite his anti-graft campaign.
Political and banking analysts said the government could not avoid responsibility for the Hanbo loan scandal due to the heavy influence of the government in banks' credit decisions and management.
Columnist Park Kwon-sang said a dramatic plunge in Kim's popularity demonstrated public distrust of his policies.

Surveys conducted after Kim's humiliating climbdown over a new labour law which was sent back to parliament last month following nearly a month of strikes showed less than 14 percent of South Koreans supported the president.
When he launched his anti-corruption campaign in 1993, Kim's popularity topped 90 percent.
"How could the honour and morality of the civilian government allow special banking treatment to a businessman with a criminal record," Park wrote in another leading newspaper Dong-a Ilbo.
Kim, the first president without a military background in 30 years, has called the close politics-business alliance a legacy of military-backed strongman rule of the past.

Chung Tae-soo, founder of the Hanbo Group, who was arrested last Friday over the loan scandal, was convicted of bribery in a multi-million dollar housing scandal involving Hanbo's construction unit in 1991.
He also paid 15 billion won ($17 million) into a slush fund raised by former president Roh Tae-woo who is now serving a 17-year jail term for corruption and human rights abuses.
"It is time for leaders of the government and (ruling) party to resign en masse to allow a new start with a fresh team," columnist Park wrote.
